item.title: Trump's opponents are planning how to reverse his changes to the presidency
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Democratic House members are writing bills to rein in a president’s emergency powers. Lawyers are strategizing about how to insulate the Justice Department from presidential influence. A House measure would block a president from unilaterally remodeling the White House. Ethicists are writing rules to prevent a future first family from self-dealing. Throughout Washington and beyond, President Donald Trump’s opponents are scrambling to ensure that after he leaves office, the changes he has imposed on the presidency, and the country, will fade with him. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Whether they succeed could determine whether Trump’s aggressive exercise of executive powers will be limited to a finite stretch of U.S. history or will instead become a model for every president to come. Rep. Jamie Raskin (Maryland), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said that Trump’s uses of presidential power can and must be reversed - but doing so will take decades. “We have a massive reconstruction task ahead of us,” Raskin said in an interview. “Fortunately, reconstruction has a great history in our country, and when it’s allowed to work, it has been a lot more successful than either authoritarianism or revolution. … We will have to go department by department, subject by subject, and public purpose by public purpose to determine what we salvage and what we re-create.” From the beginning of the republic, the three branches have jostled for control over spending, war-making, immigration and virtually every other government function. Trump is hardly the first president to try to sharply elbow the other branches out of the way. In 1981, Ronald Reagan startled critics by firing more than 11,000 air traffic controllers. George W. Bush, jolted by the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, secretly approved tactics against prisoners that many considered torture. Barack Obama, initially critical of such actions, went on to expand presidential authority in his own right. He created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in 2012 by executive order, prompting GOP complaints that he was simply making up a law. He used drone strikes to target and kill suspected terrorists far from traditional battlefields. And he put numerous “czars” over areas like energy and health care, which Republicans charged was a way to avoid confirmation fights. Tiffany Justice, executive vice president of the conservative group Heritage Action, pointed to this history to dismiss talk of post-Trump reforms, saying the president is doing nothing Democratic presidents have not done and predicting that Democrats’ plans will go nowhere. “They are full of baloney - I don’t think Democrats would ever limit the power of a Democratic president,” Justice said. “The idea of Democrats saving democracy, it’s nonsense.” Administration officials argue that Trump has changed the country forever and followed established procedures for everything he has done. “The Trump administration has abided by all legal decisions and gone through the appellate process with great success,” said a White House spokesman. “His successes on behalf of the American people will be imprinted upon the fabric of America and will be felt by every other White House that comes after him,” said White House communications director Steven Cheung. But Trump’s critics say that in the scale, sweep and sheer aggressiveness of his actions - from demolishing the East Wing of the White House to pursuing legal actions against political opponents - Trump has pushed executive authority far beyond any previous modern president. With a possible recapture of Congress just one month away, Democrats’ efforts to limit the staying power of those changes are heating up. Several lawmakers are crafting bills to curtail a president’s ability to declare emergencies, which Trump has used in novel ways, declaring about a dozen emergencies to justify policies as varied as imposing tariffs, accelerating deportations and deploying the National Guard. Reps. Suzan DelBene (D-Washington) and Don Beyer (D-Virginia) have introduced a bill forbidding a president from levying tariffs under the guise of a national emergency unless Congress agrees. Raskin has drafted bills to ban a president from accepting payments from foreign governments without Congress’s consent and require a public review for renovations of the White House. Another measure would block a president from entering monetary settlements with his own government, which a federal judge scolded Trump and the Justice Department for this summer, saying they had attempted to “use” and “manipulate” the court to legitimize a deal that would have shielded Trump from IRS scrutiny and set up a nearly $1.8 billion fund for alleged victims of politicized prosecutions. Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and potential Democratic presidential candidate, recently released an ethics proposal for all three branches of government that would ban trading stocks and betting in prediction markets, require a blind trust for anyone worth more than $1 million, and forbid individuals from accepting foreign gifts. Trump has traded millions of dollars worth of individual stocks since taking office and famously accepted the gift of an aircraft from the Qatari government. And Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut) has introduced a No Political Enemies Act, forbidding executive branch officials from prosecuting or punishing individuals or groups for their speech, something Trump has done relatively openly. Some of these proposals may be partly symbolic, aimed at galvanizing voters and showing resistance to Trump rather than serving as strict blueprints for reform. Democrats themselves do not know when, if ever, they may have the public support to push them through. They have no guarantee of success; Trump survived two impeachments, prosecutions and investigations before winning the White House a second time. Still, the Democrats say they see little alternative to trying. The Partnership for Public Service, which trains government employees and advocates for ways to improve the public workforce, has crafted proposals to strengthen civil service protections, making it harder for future presidents to fire employees en masse as Trump and his ally Elon Musk did. Congress, for example, could strengthen rules requiring that hiring and firing must be based on merit and due process - and then confront an administration that violates those rules. Would-be reformers argue that periods of excess in U.S. history often prompt waves of reform. The Gilded Age of the late 1800s gave way to the Progressive Era. The corruption of Watergate in the 1970s generated a slew of new ethics laws. It is not clear whether Americans support a new wave of reform laws. But a Pew poll last year found that 78 percent of Americans had concerns about expanding presidential power. “Throughout American history, reform follows scandal,” said Michael Waldman, president of the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University, a liberal-leaning think tank that focuses on law and democracy. “It does not always follow scandal, but that’s when it happens. I think there will be a real hunger, I hope from both parties, to write into law some of the protections that were assumed to be there before.” Some historians say many of Trump’s actions will be hard to reverse. It is far easier to smash through guardrails, they say, than to rebuild them. Most modern presidents have expanded executive power at the expense of Congress. Whether that trend continues could depend in large part on whether the legislative branch begins to reassert itself as a counterweight to the presidency. “Once we get through this nightmare, the rest of our careers will have to be devoted to reviving American progress and building institutions that endure and succeed,” Raskin said. “That is going to be the work of the rest of our lives.” The temptation for revenge - or acquiescence The midterm campaigns have spawned numerous Democratic candidates with sharply combative anti-Trump messages. If they win majorities in Congress, some Democrats could well be tempted to turn the president’s hardball tactics against him and his followers once he leaves the scene. A post-Trump president could, for example, prod the Justice Department to investigate his own political adversaries, as Trump has. “It will be very tempting for Democrats to say, ‘Oh, you think we are going to limit our abuse of the Justice Department? We don’t want to be suckers,’” Waldman said. “But I think that would be a big mistake. Everybody benefits when the rule of law is in play across the government.” More immediately, the next administration will have to decide whether to prosecute Trump officials who may have broken the law by misusing their authority. Some Democrats, for example, say the way Justice Department officials have targeted Trump’s enemies is illegal and could expose those officials to charges. Trump, in an effort to counteract such moves, has promised that before he leaves office he will preemptively pardon anyone who has come “within 200 feet” of the Oval Office, the Wall Street Journal has reported. Some liberals say Democrats should take a lesson from Trump on how to govern with force and purpose. Trump does not hesitate to take actions that skirt the edges of legality, happy to let the courts sort it out. He pressures private firms to back his policies. He issues sweeping executive orders rather than trying to persuade Congress to act. “This president litigates the way he bargains: He makes some very far-out claims, not expecting to win them all, but sort of ‘what the hell’ - that’s his theory,” said William A. Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to President Bill Clinton. “If you lose cases no other president would have dreamed of bringing, and you win a few big ones, you’re ahead of the game.” It may be tempting for future presidents to act the same way. “There has been an overcautiousness in some Democratic and some Republican administrations that will seem quite quaint after this administration,” said Ben Olinsky, senior vice president at the Center for American Progress, a center-left think tank. That is especially true of executive orders and actions, which Trump has refashioned as all-purpose policy and communications weapons. He has issued more than 280 so far in his second term, far outpacing his recent predecessors, according to figures compiled by the American Presidency Project at the University of California at Santa Barbara. “A new administration will do a lot of governing through executive order,” said Richard Pildes, a constitutional law professor at New York University. “They will want to show that they can act decisively.” Even while they plot a post-Trump future, many Democrats say they cannot simply return to a status quo that voters hated. Yet it is far from clear what their new agenda will be. Max Stier, president of the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, said the damage Trump has inflected on the current system opens up new possibilities. Stier has suggested slashing the roughly 4,000 political appointees in the government, saying they can be unqualified and unaccountable. “There is opportunity in this madness, the opportunity to reexamine some of the basic expectations around our government,” Stier said. “Because the status quo has been disrupted, the ability to think larger and bigger is there.” Tiffany Justice, of Heritage Action, challenged that entire narrative. Trump is not wielding the presidency in some new way, she said, but rather using it as Democrats always have - and that is what truly upsets the left. “President Trump is using his power in a way that Democrats have in the past,” Justice said, citing, for example, President Joe Biden’s order protecting gender transition care. “Republicans always in the past have been uneasy about using power. Democrats are never uneasy about using power.” Another Watergate? If there is anything that gives would-be reformers hope, it is the aftermath of the Watergate scandal that brought down President Richard M. Nixon. Nixon, like Trump, stretched presidential authority in ways that challenged the law and the Constitution. After his 1974 resignation, a previously quiescent Congress roared back to action, as lawmakers rushed to make sure Watergate could not happen again. Congress passed bills restricting a president’s ability to misuse private data, spy on Americans, misspend campaign cash, declare emergencies, control spending and more. Some critics envision a post-Trump America swept up in a similar reform fever, with lawmakers scrambling to score political points amid widespread public revulsion over Trump’s self-aggrandizement and self-enrichment. For example, Congress could make it illegal to do what Trump’s firebrand housing official Bill Pulte has done - accuse the president’s critics of mortgage fraud with little evidence. Or it could restrict the ability of a Federal Communications Commission chairman, like Trump’s Brendan Carr, to target outlets disliked by the president. The Justice Department is a particular focus of the would-be reformers, many of them former department lawyers frustrated by the way Trump has used DOJ to pursue his adversaries. Under Attorney General Todd Blanche, formerly Trump’s personal attorney, and his predecessor Pam Bondi, many experienced attorneys have fled the department or been forced out. Vanita Gupta, who served as associate attorney general under Biden, said Justice Department veterans of both parties are discussing how to restore the department to its former ethos of independence. “Rebuilding will be challenging, no doubt, but former DOJ officials from Republican and Democratic administrations are already thinking about how to get it done,” Gupta said. “Seasoned career leaders have told me that they would return to rebuild the department, even knowing lifetime tenure may be a thing of the past.” Historians concede the Watergate analogy has its limits. The 1974 scandal propelled Democrats to overwhelming majorities of 61-39 in the Senate and 291-144 in the House; those margins are unthinkable today. Americans have become more polarized in the past 50 years, a trend that works against any broad-based reform crusade. A powerful executive has gained additional theoretical backing in recent decades, as conservative legal scholars have advanced a “unitary executive” theory, arguing the U.S. Constitution gives the president nearly unfettered, unreviewable control over the executive branch. What the people want Ultimately, the shape of the post-Trump future will be determined by how Americans feel when he exits the stage: Will they applaud his exercise of power and attacks on long-standing structures? Or will they recoil? “The president and the courts are staring at one another over the mostly supine body of the Congress of the United States, and it’s very dangerous for constitutional government,” Galston said. The Supreme Court’s path is unclear as well. Some Democrats privately echo a sentiment voiced by Clinton - that the justices may not give future presidents the same leeway they have accorded Trump. The court has already been far more deferential to Trump than it was to Biden, these Democrats say. “I have a sinking suspicion if our party wins the White House in the next election, there will be a hallelujah moment and the Supreme Court will rediscover the Constitution,” Clinton said on ABC’s “The View” last year. Even if some curbs on presidential power are reestablished, Trump’s demonstration that they can be dismantled is likely to have long-term effects. Young people might be less willing to work for a government whose policies vacillate wildly from one president to another, and where long tenure is not guaranteed. Foreign allies have made it clear they are far less trusting of Washington’s commitments. Businesses and nonprofits could be less interested in accepting funding they fear could be abruptly withdrawn. “It’s not like a toggle switch that you can just turn it on and off,” Waldman said. “Much of the federal government took a century to build.” Some historians note Trump’s unique qualities, saying his combination of celebrity, aggressiveness and disregard for tradition is unlikely ever to be replicated. That suggests future presidents cannot simply repeat his performance, they say. “Any thought that [Vice President] JD Vance or [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio gets to be president and do the same thing with the same abandon - I don’t see that happening,” said John Lawrence, a historian and former top aide to former House speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-California). “He has created his own unitary executive theory, and I don’t know how it works outside the size and force of the personality of Donald Trump. But that doesn’t mean a Republican successor wouldn’t try.” In the Progressive Era, Americans took to the streets by the thousands to demand reform, Stier said, and if Trump’s changes are ultimately reversed, it will be because of a similar groundswell. “The most important question we face is whether we can return to a consensus that we had among Republicans, Democrats and independents for 140 years that an operating government of our values requires leaders committed to the public good, not the private interests of the officeholder of the day,” Stier said. “Can we get back to that? I think the answer is yes. But we need a public that demands it.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/04/democrats-are-making-plans-clean-up-government-post-trump-era/

item.title: Poll shows Latino voters swinging away from Trump and Republicans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NBC News Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in a 2026 election that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations. Like the broader electorate , Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living. NBC News There are clear signs his party is paying the price. A greater share of Latino voters hold negative views of the Republican Party than at any time since 2016, and Democrats have leads on issues like dealing with the economy, immigration, the cost of living, corruption and healthcare. Two years ago, Latino voters gave Trump a 4-point edge over then-Vice President Kamala Harris on handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question. Against that backdrop, Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%. That’s double the lead they had among Latino voters at this point in 2024, though not quite at the heights the party enjoyed at this time in 2018, according to NBC News polling from just before that election. Nearly a fifth of Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 say they do not prefer a Republican-controlled Congress, with 14% saying they support Democrats and 8% unsure in their preference. The shifts come after the Republican Party made Trump’s 2024 gains among Latino voters central to its plans to keep the House majority. In Florida and Texas, the party drew new, heavily Latino districts that looked deep red by the 2024 results — but many are shaping up to be competitive in the midterms as Latino voters’ preferences have changed. Statewide races in Texas, Nevada and more will also be shaped by the evolving Latino vote, though it will not move as one bloc everywhere in the country. The poll results, collected Sept. 21-28, “indicate a striking reversal of Republican gains with Latino voters and point to trouble ahead for Republican candidates in the midterms,” said Democratic pollster Aileen Cardona-Arroyo of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the poll with Republican pollster Micah Roberts and his firm, Public Opinion Strategies. Latino voters comprised around a tenth of the total vote in recent midterm elections. Roberts referred to Latino voters as “the swingiest of swing groups,” calling the reversal since 2024 “stunning.” “What we can really say from this data is that 2024 was the outlier,” he said, adding: “Trump is a central figure. He’s had real consequences on our politics, and without his presence, I think none of these changes would be evident in the data among Latinos.” But the results among Latino voters are not all good news for Democrats, who have not seen their party’s image improve in two years. And while Democrats have a midterm lead, Republicans are pulling more Latino support than in any NBC News poll before the 2024 election cycle, too, dating back to 2012. “Despite a more favorable environment for Democrats, any Democratic gains this November will be driven largely more by opposition to Trump and the economic environment than by support for Democrats,” Arroyo-Cardona said. Trump struggles Latino voters overwhelmingly disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living (78%), the economy (74%), foreign policy (68%) and immigration (69%). Trump’s best issue of the five tested is border security — where 39% approve and 58% disapprove of his handling. His marks on foreign policy, the economy and cost of living are significantly lower than where then-President Joe Biden sat with Latino voters in September 2022, when Democrats had a better-than-expected midterm result despite losing control of the House. Then, 60% disapproved of Biden’s handling of the cost of living and 54% disapproved of his handling of the economy. Nearly two-thirds (65%) of Latino voters say the president’s policies have hurt economic conditions, compared with 23% who say his policies have helped and 11% who say they haven’t made much of a difference. Among Latino independents, just 10% believe his policies have helped the economy, while 72% believe his policies have hurt it. Meanwhile, inflation and the cost of living ranked as the most important issue to 33% of Latino voters. That made it the top issue in the survey — and a majority (52%) ranked it as the most or second-most important issue. Latino voters who say the cost of living is the most important issue also prefer a Democratic Congress by 22 points. That’s a shift from the 2024 poll, when Republicans had a 4-point edge among these voters. A sizable majority of Latinos (63%) say their family’s income is falling behind the cost of living, while 25% say it is staying even and 11% say it is going up faster than the cost of living, similar to findings in 2024. Luisa Santiago, a 59-year-old Florida retiree who participated in the survey, told NBC News in a subsequent interview that she voted for Trump in 2024 after a lifetime of voting for Democrats and convinced many of her friends to do the same. She was frustrated with the Democrats on the economy and on transgender issues. “It was a big deal when we voted for Republicans, and then we feel like it was a complete mistake,” she said, calling Trump a “disappointment.” “I’m more embarrassed than my friends because I was the one who convinced them to vote for him,” she added. Santiago lambasted the president’s deportation policies as “brutal” and “cold,” while also saying the difficult economic climate is weighing heavily on her and her family. While immigration didn’t rank as highly on the priority list, Latino voters expressed similar frustration with Trump’s hard-edged deportation policies. Two-thirds say Trump’s immigration enforcement measures have gone too far, 22% say he’s struck the right approach, and 9% say he hasn’t gone far enough. While 83% support deporting all undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, just 37% support deporting every undocumented immigrant in the U.S. Roberts, the Republican pollster, pointed to the difference between support for deporting serious criminals and deporting everyone in America illegally as he imagined “what might have been” for Republicans. “There is support for a certain level of immigration enforcement, but the Latino electorate believes it’s gone way too far,” he added. In the poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years. Eighteen percent say they or someone close to them has considered leaving the U.S. over the last two years over concerns about ICE enforcement, and 17% say they or someone close to them has considered not voting in person this year because of concerns about ICE. Maria, a Florida voter in her 20s who responded to the poll, told NBC News in a follow-up interview that Trump has “fallen short” in the two years since she voted for him. She declined to share her last name while discussing politics. She highlighted frustration on the economy and on deportations, arguing that while Trump promised to deport the worst of the worst, “I’ve had many friends, family members deported.” “They were supposed to be here. They had paperwork, and it didn’t matter. And now they can never come back. One of my friend’s grandpas didn’t even get deported to his home country. He got deported to Mexico instead of Cuba,” she later added. Midterms fallout The numbers for Trump and Republicans could spell trouble in November in states and districts with sizable Latino populations. “In a lot of the heavily Hispanic and Latino districts across the country that Trump and Republicans did well, and better than ever in, in 2024, you’re going to see that reversal,” said Roberts, the Republican pollster, noting Trump’s tough numbers on immigration and the cost of living. “This entire poll is full of very clear directional signals that Latinos have turned from 2024 and are ready to make a different choice with regard to who’s in control of Congress,” Roberts said. Democrats’ 24-point lead on the generic congressional ballot is twice as large as their margin in the 2024 version of the poll. But it’s not nearly as wide as the 43-point lead the party enjoyed at this point in the 2018 midterms. Latino voters also now say Democrats would better handle the cost of living and the economy by significant margins, erasing the advantages Trump and Republicans have enjoyed in past elections. Latino voters favor Democrats to handle other issues, and they break even on which party would better handle border security. More voters also say Democrats are more likely than Republicans to share their values and address the concerns of the Hispanic community. Amid the economic frustrations, voters are also more motivated to head to the polls in November. A sizable majority (72%) rank themselves a 10 out of 10 in terms of interest in November’s elections, compared with 54% at this time in 2024. Meanwhile, 62% say they are more motivated to vote this year than in midterms past. And a majority (54%) say their midterm vote is meant to send a signal of opposition to Trump, while 21% say they want to signal their support for Trump and 23% say their vote is not about sending a signal to the president either way. While the poll results offer plenty of short-term upside for Democrats, they also outline longer-term changes trending against the party. While Latino voters’ negative views of the GOP have jumped since 2024, views of the Democratic Party have not improved. Now, 62% of Latino voters have negative views of the Republican Party, a 16-point increase from two years ago, while 42% have a negative view of the Democratic Party, a 4-point increase from 2024. “I’m still wary about the Democratic Party because I don’t really know that much other than what I was fed,” said Maria, the Florida voter in her 20s, before adding that she’s still leaning toward voting for Democrats: “I feel like I have to put my faith in them now to fix things.” She said she voted for Trump in 2024 in large part because her family instilled a fear of socialism and Democrats in her. The poll found that socialism remains underwater with Latino voters — 13% feel positively about it and 41% view socialism negatively, with 38% feeling neutral about socialism. Cardona-Arroyo, the Democratic pollster, noted that the party has work to do after the midterms to develop a broader message. “What do Democrats do to move beyond this place where they’re running on opposition to the Republican Party, which I think will work in ’26?” Cardona-Arroyo said. “It’s sort of an open question of whether that will work in ’28.” The NBC News/Telemundo poll surveyed 800 registered Latino voters Sept. 21-28 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text messages. Overall, 20% of the interviews were conducted in Spanish. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. item.title: Trump names Jay Clayton as AI czar: Where he stands on AI safety
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump on Sunday named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as his new "AI czar," adding a different category of intelligence, the "artificial" kind, to the U.S. spy chief's portfolio. In a post on Truth Social , Trump said Clayton will lead a newly formed "Super Intelligence Force" alongside Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael and Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor. The group will report directly to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its goal, Trump wrote, is "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution, and the Internet, and will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans." Clayton will keep his job as DNI, which oversees the nation's 18 intelligence agencies. Trump's announcement follows meeting last Tuesday at the White House where top AI executives signed what he called a " morally binding " agreement to police themselves in order to prevent their increasingly powerful models from going rogue and harming humanity . "There's a belief that there should be tremendous self-regulation," the president said at the meeting. "This is going to be all for the good, and we're going to have it be nice and safe." Despite new polls showing that 86% of Americans want AI companies to meet independent safety standards even if doing so slows development — with 74% largely mistrusting the leaders of those companies — Trump insisted in recent days that federal regulations are unnecessary and that those who say otherwise are " Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers ." "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote on social media . Elsewhere, Trump has said that regulation would handicap the U.S. in its race to "win" AI. "Whoever wins AI ... that's the group that wins," Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month . "We're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way." According to the Guardian , Trump's previous AI and crypto czar, billionaire tech investor David Sacks, consistently "counseled the president to give a soft touch to AI regulation, helping push executive orders and other measures aimed at loosening restrictions on the technology." Sacks also "maintains direct financial stakes in multiple AI companies," the paper reported, though he took steps to divest some of his holdings last year while serving in the administration. He stepped down in March. Will Clayton follow Sacks's lead? Or will he chart a new course? Here's what we know so far. Who is Jay Clayton? Clayton, 60, is a registered independent with degrees from the University of Pennsylvania (engineering, law) and the University of Cambridge (economics). As a lawyer in private practice, he focused mostly on Wall Street: mergers and acquisitions, market offerings and regulatory proceedings. During Trump's first term, from 2017 to 2020, Clayton chaired the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. From March 2021 to April 2025, Clayton served as chair and "lead independent director" of the board of Apollo Global Management . (Apollo has owned a 90% majority stake in Yahoo since September 2021.) In late 2024, Trump nominated Clayton to serve as U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, his first prosecutorial job; Trump later appointed Clayton to serve in an acting capacity after New York Sen. Chuck Schumer blocked his appointment. Reports suggest Clayton was also considered for roles as secretary of the treasury, attorney general and director of the Central Intelligence Agency. In November 2025, Trump ordered the Department of Justice to investigate Democrats associated with Jeffrey Epstein, and U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi assigned Clayton to lead the probe . After former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard resigned in May 2026, Trump tapped Clayton to replace her. "He's very qualified," Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia said at the time . But Clayton sidestepped questions over who won the 2020 election during his July confirmation hearings, and he was confirmed without Democratic support. "I'm not an election denier," Clayton told the Senate. "He went through our processes, and Joe Biden became the president of the United States." What has Clayton said about AI? During his DNI confirmation hearings, Clayton described AI as "a game changer ," warning that it represents "not only an opportunity but a threat." "We should just all recognize that," he continued. "When something is both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it." On Tuesday, Clayton attended Trump's White House meeting with top AI executives. Speaking afterward to CNBC, he used the president's new preferred term for AI — i.e., "superintelligence " — while pushing back against lawmakers who have called for regulating or pausing U.S. AI development. "Super intelligence is a national security issue, and that was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders but everybody in the room," Clayton said. "But to, in some way, not try to drive forward inside the United States, with companies that are regulated in the United States ... to somehow say we should back away from this and let the rest of the world develop these models and implement these models? I don't think anybody in that room, and I don't think any American, should think that that's a good strategy." Asked to respond to criticism from Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts that Trump's current policy of letting AI companies police themselves will prove to be "a recipe for disaster," Clayton suggested that the U.S. government's existing regulatory framework could also help keep AI in check. "My response to the American people on that front is we have a Federal Trade Commission, we have a Department of Justice," Clayton said. "I know the leaders of both those organizations, and they're committed to protecting the American people in this regard." What will Clayton do as AI czar? According to Trump's post, the Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the federal government's dealings with AI companies, infrastructure providers, consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, CNN reported . Last month, Trump wrote on social media that he would "be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar.' "Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!" he added. In the same post, the president again dismissed concerns about AI safety as a "hoax" perpetrated by "Radical Left Democrats." He also wrote that going forward, his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," which he described as "the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet" — only "even larger and more impactful." "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!" Trump explained. As for reining in "bad" actors, he wrote, "we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System." Clayton, it seems, will now be in charge of cherishing, helping and watching over the AI industry as it grows. He's "a good man," Trump told Axios when the outlet asked last week if Clayton was being considered for the job . "He's right here. That's a good idea." It's unclear what happened to a separate idea Trump floated last month, which he called "the AI Force." "I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force , which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term," Trump wrote in his September social media post about naming an AI czar. According to Axios , Trump's AI Force idea "caught advisers by surprise," setting off "a mad dash" within the administration "to imagine what AI Force would look like." What did Trump's previous AI czar do? When Sacks served as AI czar, he repeatedly persuaded the president and his administration to resist new AI restrictions, including state laws to limit AI . Since leaving the White House, Sacks has "maintained close ties with the president," according to the Guardian, and "in May, he successfully urged Trump to scrap an executive order that would've subjected AI models to government review." The Wall Street Journal recently reported the Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles were "caught off guard and unhappy" with Trump's decision after they "spent months negotiating to increase oversight of AI and had consulted a range of industry executives on the order." According to the Journal's sources, Wiles "told others that Sacks had persuaded Trump" to back down "in a last-minute call," leaving Bessent "worried that AI-led cyberattacks could wreak havoc on the nation's banking system." item.title: Iran tells U.S. there is no military solution to Middle East war
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ships anchored off the coast of Musandam governorate in Oman near the Strait of Hormuz on Friday (-) Iran's top diplomat insisted on Sunday that there would be no military solution to the United States' war against the Islamic republic, with talks on ending the conflict apparently at an impasse. A campaign of heavy bombardment failed to bring a decisive close to the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, and Washington in recent weeks has dialled back military operations in favour of economic pressure. The main point of contention remains Iran's attempt to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, a vital conduit for Gulf oil and gas where a UK maritime agency reported on Sunday another tanker was struck by an unknown projectile. "If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a gathering of foreign ambassadors. "There is no military solution, nor any solution based on new sanctions," he continued, adding "only negotiations based on justice and fairness" could end the conflict. The two sides agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Hormuz prompted a return to US military operations. Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorisation. The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports, and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it. On Sunday, the British maritime security agency UKMTO said a tanker in the Hormuz "reported being struck by an unknown projectile, causing damage to the engine room", though the crew were reported safe and no environmental impact was recorded. The agency did not specify the date of the incident, the vessel's origin or destination, or whether it was an oil tanker or LNG carrier. In Iran, oil minister Mohsen Paknejad has resigned, the president's office said on Sunday, as the US maintains a blockade on the country's oil exports. In a news bulletin on the minister's resignation, state television ran an interview with an official from the Iranian presidential office who said Paknejad initially offered to quit a while ago "due to personal issues" but this was rejected. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had asked Paknejad to continue in his post but was now accepting his departure as the minister had insisted on leaving, the official added. Paknejad has been replaced by Hamid Bovard, the chief executive of the National Iranian Oil Company, the presidency said. - Focused on Hormuz - Iranian and US officials last week held indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, with Tehran saying it presented seven conditions for reopening the strait. Iran has demanded, among other things, a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of its assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade. Trump, however, rejected the proposal, while leaving the door open both to further talks or renewed military operations. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Sunday that the US had expressed its views on the proposal and said they were being reviewed. "The Americans, through intermediaries, have also conveyed their views on this proposal, and these views are currently being examined inside the country through the relevant channels and procedures," he told reporters, according to state news agency IRNA. "Whenever the final position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is ready, appropriate steps will be taken accordingly. At the same time, the Islamic Republic of Iran is also preparing itself for any other possible scenario." Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Sunday characterised the latest US counterproposal as being "in line with their previous proposals concerning nuclear issues". "We have clearly indicated that we are focusing on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz," he said, adding that reopening the waterway required "an end to the disruptions to Iranian commercial maritime traffic and the lifting of sanctions". The United States and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons -- a goal it has long denied pursuing -- though the focus soon shifted to reopening the Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through world energy markets. The United States has not struck Iran since September 1, but it has recently pursued a fresh military buildup in the region. ap-sbr/smw/axn/jfx/amj This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/iran-tells-us-no-military-094635228.html

item.title: Sam Altman says the world should accept 'some bad things' for AI's benefits
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there remains a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology’s benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public. “I think there's a lot of daylight,” Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter-touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI backing tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models. Altman agreed with Amodei’s call last month to slow the development of the most advanced AI models. His company has followed Anthropic in endorsing new state laws that impose stricter safety requirements than what the maker of ChatGPT had previously supported — a subtle shift from its prior state strategy . And OpenAI lobbyists recently endorsed a bipartisan House proposal that would require top AI companies to embed outside safety evaluators. Despite the convergence, Altman tried to distinguish his firm’s regulatory stance from Anthropic’s, referencing a criticism about regulatory capture that tech advisers close to President Donald Trump have applied to Anthropic. “I disagree, but I understand the perspective of people who are like, ‘This technology is going to get so powerful, and it’s so dangerous, that a single lab in San Francisco should have it and make sure nothing bad happens, and kind of figure out how to dole out the benefits,’” said Altman. He called it “a completely unacceptable trade-off” that runs counter to the “lighter-touch regulatory stance” backed by OpenAI. “I wouldn't take a trade of saying, ‘We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,’” said Altman. “Because I think people will do tremendously — orders of magnitude more — good stuff than bad stuff.” The OpenAI CEO later added that he does not accept “the really catastrophic risks,” including the potential for “a serious loss of control to AI.” Asked to respond, an Anthropic spokesperson said that its “regulatory proposals apply only to frontier models.” The company also referred to an August social media exchange that Amodei had with an investment manager, addressing criticisms around regulatory capture and impacts on smaller companies. “Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully,” Amodei said at the time. “We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors.” The Altman interview, appearing in Monday’s debut edition of Decoded and its accompanying daily podcast, also delved into Trump’s new AI accord with top tech firms and his attempted “superintelligence” rebrand; the rash of autonomous hacking incidents carried out by OpenAI models and whether the company should face legal liability; Altman’s thoughts on the AI industry money swamping U.S. politics; the influence of so-called effective altruists inside OpenAI; and his views on key political power players including French President Emmanuel Macron and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Decoded by POLITICO — produced by Brendan, Christine Mui, Calder McHugh and Sam Sutton — draws on the reporting of some 50 POLITICO journalists around the world to cover not just where tech is going, but the personalities, policy fights and political battles taking it there. item.title: FBI arrests suspected Chinese agent accused of surveilling Taiwan president's son
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The FBI arrested a suspected Chinese agent at Los Angeles International Airport after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese president's U.S.-based son, law enforcement sources told CBS News. Wanying "Heather" Zhang, an Irvine, California, realtor, was cuffed by federal law enforcement on Sunday before she boarded a flight to Shanghai, China, from LAX, on a charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. Zhang's husband Edric Ding, a realtor at the same firm, told CBS News when reached by phone Sunday: "I don't know anything yet," and declined to comment further. It was not immediately clear if Zhang has an attorney. A criminal complaint, filed in federal court by a member of the FBI's counterintelligence squad in L.A., accused Zhang and an accomplice of traveling to Seattle, Washington, in September 2025 and taking pictures at the suburban home of a top Taiwanese official's family. Law enforcement sources told CBS News that the target was Ting-Yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Ching-Te Lai. Ting-Yu, an engineer in his 30s, attended college in America and has a young U.S.-born son with his wife, Hsiao Chen, according to Taiwanese media reports. He now works for the Dutch multinational electronics firm Philips. "If the PRC [People's Republic of China] wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to the PRC," wrote FBI Special Agent Kevin Holt in the Oct. 3, 2026, criminal complaint. Taiwan has been the focus of high geopolitical tensions for decades . It asserts its independence, while the Chinese government claims it is part of China. The island is in a key position astride major shipping lanes, and is where many of the world's most advanced semiconductor chips are manufactured. CBS News reached out to the Taiwanese consulate for comment. The complaint said Zhang, 34, and a man named only as "Individual 1" flew from Las Vegas to Seattle on Sept. 1, 2025, rented a black Nissan Rogue and drove to their target's home. Images from a neighbor's security camera included in the complaint allegedly show the two "appearing to film" Ting-Yu, his wife and their child as they arrived home that evening. CBS News matched the images to an address near Seattle owned by Ting-Yu. Zhang allegedly texted her Chinese government handler: "Saw him. Young male. It's that young one," and "I am videorecording," followed by two license plate numbers, according to the complaint. The FBI agent wrote that the texts from the Chinese messaging app WeChat were obtained from a search warrant on Zhang's iCloud account. "Zhang was in contact with at least two people whom she appeared to acknowledge worked for the PRC government," the agent wrote. The complaint claims Zhang was introduced in June 2025 to one of the Chinese government officials by a classmate from her alma mater, Beijing's University of International Relations, which Holt said has close ties to the Ministry of State Security. Holt's affidavit claims Zhang booked a private room in Changsha, China, during a June 2025 trip, where she allegedly met the government official and received her surveillance mission. She later texted the official, "I can take care of this thing," according to the complaint. On Aug. 26, 2025, Zhang wrote: "I will be busy with work in L.A. this week. I will probably go to Seattle next week," and the official replied: "Ok. Thank you for your hard work," the complaint said. Zhang is a licensed California realtor with JC Pacific Capital Inc. Her Zillow profile says she has 130 sales and listings around Los Angeles and neighboring counties. Ting-Yu received his bachelor's in electrical engineering from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio, in 2012; a master's in Bioengineering Innovation and Design from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, the following year; then a PhD from the Department of Bioengineering at the University of Washington, according to a profile from one of his academic publications. Taiwan TV news station SETN reported that he met his Taiwanese wife while studying for his doctorate. They married in 2018 and had a child in the U.S. in 2020, according to CNA , Taiwan's national news agency. Chinese government agents have previously been caught spying on and harassing Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists in the U.S. Federal prosecutors said Shujun Wang , 75, infiltrated and informed on a Chinese pro-democracy group in Queens, New York, for the Chinese Ministry of State Security for 17 years. He was convicted in 2024 of acting as a foreign agent. Two people were arrested in April 2023 for their involvement in an unofficial Chinese police station in Manhattan set up to monitor Chinese dissidents. The Justice Department has warned of a plan by the Chinese security services called Operation Fox Hunt aimed at repatriating wanted Chinese nationals around the world, which targets enemies of the regime. New York-based Quanzhong An, who prosecutors say is a leader of the U.S. wing of Operation Fox Hunt, was sentenced in March 2025 after harassing a Chinese dissident in an attempt to bring them back to China. In California, former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang was charged with acting as a Chinese agent in May. She admitted to being paid to spread pro-Chinese government propaganda in the U.S., including an essay on her blog denying "forced labor" in China. item.title: Heating oil costs could jump 50% this winter and add nearly $900 to bills
item.description:

The ongoing global energy crunch doesn't just cause pain at the gas pump: As winter approaches, millions of Americans are facing dramatic spikes in their home heating costs. The price of heating oil, which some 4.8 million households, mostly in the Northeast and Alaska, use to heat their homes, is approaching all-time highs as two wars strain global supply. Heating oil costs are expected to jump 50% this winter, according to one estimate from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, adding nearly $900 to the average home's heating bill. The jump is catching consumers by surprise at a time of year when many households fill their tanks for winter, and it's stoking concern that the high prices will force low-income families to make tough choices between warming their homes and paying for necessities. Read more: What an extended war with Iran could mean for gas prices "There's a lot of sticker shock," said Chris Herb, president of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association, a trade group for local fuel providers and other energy companies in the state. Heating oil is nearly identical to diesel, and diesel prices have continued to rise while crude oil prices have plateaued as higher seasonal demand collides with ongoing supply shocks. The Iran War has disrupted exporters' ability to reliably pass through the Strait of Hormuz, while escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries have limited another key source of supply. Read more: How to protect your money as Mideast turmoil fuels market volatility Record-high prices In recent weeks, diesel prices have topped $6.50 a gallon, breaking an all-time record. And across the Northeastern states, heating oil prices have either recently broken or are just short of the highest levels on record. "Diesel and heating oil are basically directly tied now," said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. "Diesel setting all-time records is certainly very worrisome for home heating oil expenses this winter." Heating oil costs are expected to jump 50% this winter, according to one estimate from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. (AP Photo/Robert F. Bukaty) ASSOCIATED PRESS A gallon of heating oil now averages around $5.96 in Maine, where more than half the state relies on oil, the highest share anywhere in the country. Prices are $5.87 in Vermont and $5.91 in Connecticut, meaning 100 gallons, a common minimum order threshold, comes out to nearly $600. During the winter months, a typical home relying on heating oil alone can run through 100 gallons in a few weeks. Homeowners have been making tough choices: Fill up now, or hold off in hopes that prices fall in the months ahead? Look into alternative heating sources that might be pricey up front but deliver savings in the long-term? Lower the thermostat and shiver to stretch a tank's worth of oil longer? 'Do I order? Do I hold off?' In Connecticut, Herb said suppliers were seeing more business than is typical for September, perhaps a sign that households who had been waiting in vain for prices to go down after February's Iran war shock didn't want to risk another price jump later in the season. KC, who lives near Augusta, Maine, and asked that her last name be withheld to protect her privacy, recently made a similar calculation. She was just quoted $5.99 per gallon for her 100-gallon order and could end up paying even more if prices are higher when her delivery arrives. In a typical year, she pays closer to $3 a gallon. "I was shocked, honestly, to find out that oil was this much," the 51-year-old said. She knew prices had been rising, but didn't realize the extent of the jump until a month ago, when a colleague at her healthcare job mentioned paying around $5 a gallon. "That's when I started thinking, 'Do I order? Do I hold off?'" she said. "I really didn't think it would get this bad." Meanwhile, she's taking several other steps to reduce her heating costs. She'll set her thermostat to 50 — the lowest she thinks she can go without risking a pipe freeze — and rely primarily on her two pellet stoves for heat. She's also looking into sealing her windows with plastic insulation and adding fans to help heat circulate more evenly throughout her home. Weatherization measures and system tune-ups can shave up to 10% off a typical bill, Herb said. "Ten percent at these levels is meaningful, meaningful money back in your pocket," he said. Options also exist for those who need help with rising energy bills. The federally funded Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program provides grants to qualifying households, and many states also have similar programs for low- and moderate-income families. But with costs so high this year, politicians, industry watchers, and worried neighbors alike have all expressed concerns about how lower-income households and elderly people who rely on fixed incomes will manage, and if the existing programs are enough. A bipartisan group of senators is pressuring the Trump administration to release this year's assistance funds early, and several bills aimed at expanding the program have been introduced. Meanwhile, Maine Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King have requested that President Trump tap the federal government's 1 million-barrel emergency supply of heating oil "to protect Mainers from the very high prices that are imposing a difficult financial burden." After he lost, he certified the results as “full, true and correct.” Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. He nonetheless harbored doubts. Some ballots smelled too inky, he said. Some seemed too heavy. Some felt too rough. He stashed the ballots in a storage room, slapped a padlock on the door, ordered subordinates to destroy the keys and reported his suspicions to President Donald Trump’s administration. In another place or era, Curtis’s concerns would be dismissed as kooky. But in Shasta County in 2026, they have been taken seriously enough to spur FBI agents to show up with bolt cutters so they could take a look. For years, Shasta County has been a center of election denialism. Citing debunked conspiracy theories about voting machines, its conservative county supervisors dumped their contract with Dominion Voting Systems and toyed with counting ballots by hand. Activists sued over election practices. And during this summer’s election, voters approved a measure that would require photo ID to vote, restrict mail ballots and mandate hand counts - policies that courts have blocked. Shasta County offers a glimpse of what happens when distrust in elections takes root in a community. Across the United States, both Democrats and Republicans have seen their confidence in elections wane, especially when their side loses. In Shasta County, the doubts run so deep that some residents don’t trust the results even when the candidates they back prevail. Curtis has spent a quarter century warning about rigged elections. Last year, a majority on Shasta County’s board that shared his suspicions appointed him to finish out the term of a retiring registrar of voters. Curtis sought a full term this summer, but voters in this forested county south of Mount Shasta rejected him. Since then, he has called the election into doubt in any way he can. He has questioned whether some ballots contained bamboo fibers, echoing a baseless claim from the 2020 election that counterfeit ballots in Arizona were shipped in from Asia. “I have ballots that are rougher,” Curtis said. “And I’ve been told that the bamboo fiber stuff would make it rougher. Do I know that’s true? I don’t know that’s true.” In January, Curtis will step down so his successor can take over. In the meantime, he has one more election to run as registrar, in November. And the doubts about voting in this county are unlikely to end even when Curtis leaves. Curtis’s backers are committed to scrutinizing past elections and remaking how future ones are conducted. Among them is Patrick Jones, the former county supervisor most responsible for bringing Curtis to California. Jones, 58, lost his reelection bid two years ago, and he has refused to accept his defeat. “I don’t feel like - 2024 - that I lost that race,” Jones said. “But then, how do you prove it, right? That’s a whole other thing. How do you prove what you feel?” A new leader for elections Jones, a conservative activist who helps run his family’s gun shop, won his 2020 race by capitalizing on anger over covid restrictions. His attention soon after shifted to how elections are run in the reliably Republican county. He believes even his own winning race was manipulated to lower his victory margin by unknown forces. He hasn’t turned up evidence, but his suspects include foreign actors, state figures, local workers or a combination of all of them. For six years, he and his allies have looked for ways to overhaul Shasta County’s elections and replace the people who run them. They found an opening when Cathy Darling Allen retired in 2024 after nearly two decades as registrar. She had been diagnosed with heart failure, and the stress of nonstop criticism was contributing to the decline of her health, she said. “Some local rabble-rousers decided that Trump was right and that if they don’t like the result, that means the election is rigged,” said Darling Allen, 57. “That is profoundly un-American and unpatriotic.” Jones wanted to give the job to Curtis, but a fellow conservative supervisor insisted on Tom Toller, a former prosecutor with his own doubts about elections. Jones agreed to hire him but soon felt betrayed because Toller said he found no signs of fraud and kept many of the county’s longtime election policies. Ten months after taking the job, Toller stepped down in April 2025 because of health problems. Jones was off the county board by then, but he and his allies saw a fresh shot to put a sufficiently skeptical official in charge of elections. On a 3-2 vote, the supervisors hired Curtis. ‘I neutered the machines’ Curtis came to Shasta County from Florida, and he said he moved across the country for the job because he wanted to revamp elections in a way that other communities might replicate. He had never run an election before, but he had spent more than two decades scrutinizing them after concluding that voting machines could throw off results. He wrote computer code in 2000 to show voting machines could alter results, he said, and he took his concerns to a congressional committee led by Democrats four years later. He became an immigration attorney but also continued to focus on voting machines, both as a lawyer and as a Democratic congressional candidate. Curtis, 68, usually wears a suit and tie, even on stiflingly hot days. A holster on his hip holds three cellphones. Because of his Baptist upbringing, he doesn’t drink, smoke or curse. He avoids reading media accounts of his activity, he said, even in friendly publications. Curtis started out as a Republican but said he became a Democrat when he grew disillusioned with the Bush family’s version of the GOP. He returned to the Republican Party when Trump began transforming it. Throughout his political conversions, one belief never changed: Cheating is rampant. Independent reviews have found no widespread fraud in voting, by machine or otherwise. But those studies didn’t satisfy Curtis, who suspects the 2016 election was rigged in Trump’s favor and that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. As registrar of voters, Curtis sought to alleviate fears of ballot stuffing by shutting down nine of the 13 drop boxes where county residents deposit their ballots. He hired fellow election skeptics. He removed a barrier separating election observers from county workers. He decked out the observation area in U.S. flags, making it look more like a Fourth of July celebration than a government office. His signature achievement, he said, was mounting cellphones over employee workstations to film ballots before and after they are fed into tabulators. Online viewers can conduct their own tallies and compare them with the official count, he said. “I neutered the machines,” he said. His supporters say the setup gives them more confidence in the count. His critics call it political theater, noting that some ballots aren’t filmed and that the live stream has at times crashed. Inside the office, Curtis has repeatedly clashed with longtime employees, prompting two personnel investigations. One found he probably threatened employees by saying he would throat-punch them, slap them or have them pulled out of the office by the hair. Curtis denied making such statements and has pledged to sue the county and his accusers for millions of dollars. “These are some of the worst people on the planet, in my opinion,” he said of a contingent of county employees. “And so, I will have no qualms at all about bankrupting them.” ‘Stand up for what’s right’ His most consequential disputes were with Joanna Francescut, the assistant registrar of voters. Francescut cares so much about her line of work that she planned a pregnancy to ensure she could perform her duties on Election Day in 2012. (A couple of months later, a surprise special election meant she wound up working on Election Day near her due date, and she had to leave that morning to give birth to a son.) For years, she enjoyed giving voters tours of her office and showing them how elections work, she said. Then came 2020. After Trump lost, visitors who once thanked her came with hostile questions. She set up training sessions for election observers only to find attendees exploiting them to criticize how she did her job. The county supervisors didn’t trust her either. When they got rid of voting machines and moved toward hand counts, she told them she would need more staff and more money. They didn’t believe her figures but had to abandon their plans when the state legislature passed a law requiring machine tallies. The supervisors twice declined to appoint Francescut as the registrar of voters, passing her over for candidates who had not run elections before. When they named Curtis to the job, she announced she was running for the job in the next election. Within weeks, Curtis fired her as his top assistant, saying he could dismiss her because she was an at-will employee. Francescut, 44, responded with a wrongful termination lawsuit that remains ongoing. Getting passed over for the job frustrated her, but she refused to give up, she said, because she didn’t want to send the wrong message to her teen daughter. “I can’t allow her to watch me get stomped on by men that are lying about me and not stand up for what’s right,” she said. This June, she beat Curtis in the race for registrar of voters with 58 percent of the vote. She will take office in January. His last election That left Curtis with an unusually long seven-month period as a lame duck. Curtis did not just lose the election; he lost allies. Kevin Crye, a supervisor who voted to hire Curtis, lost his own race in June. Chris Kelstrom, another supervisor who voted to hire Curtis, now says he trusts Curtis “less than gas station sushi” and accused him of creating an “HR nightmare.” In August, Kelstrom joined a board majority in censuring Curtis over the personnel investigations. Curtis said he needs help running November’s election, so he offered a job to Tina Peters, a former county clerk from Colorado convicted of four felonies for allowing an outsider to copy voting machine software in an attempt to prove the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. Peters is a hero and martyr to election skeptics, and she has been touring the country to warn of rigged elections since Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence this summer. The job offer made national headlines and angered election officials from both parties across the country. Peters turned Curtis down, saying she wanted to keep a national focus. Last month, after Curtis questioned the ballots, he received a grand jury subpoena telling him to bring them to Sacramento, he said. The subpoena was canceled, he said, after FBI agents and officials with the California secretary of state’s office visited Shasta County to interview him and inspect the boxes of ballots. County supervisors have called Curtis’s claims about the June election frivolous and said they welcome any state or federal review of the election. The FBI declined to comment. The secretary of state’s office said representatives recently went to Shasta County but declined to provide other details. Now, Curtis is preparing to run his last election for Shasta County. His detractors are worried about how he will do his job. His backers fear Francescut will reverse the changes Curtis has made. “We want truth, we want honesty, we want a fair and transparent election,” said Rich Gallardo, a Curtis ally who has spent years deriding the county’s election practices. “And we’re willing to keep fighting. I don’t know how much longer we can keep it up, but we’re willing to fight for it.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/04/shasta-countys-election-chief-lost-then-he-locked-up-ballots/

item.title: Trump’s judicial legacy will last decades. The ages of his nominees explains why.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump has appointed far more federal judges who are under 40 than his predecessors — ensuring that his imprint on the judiciary will last for decades. Over the course of his two terms to date, Trump has appointed 31 people in their 30s to federal judgeships, and at least two more are pending in the Senate, according to a POLITICO analysis of government data. By contrast, President Joe Biden appointed 13 people in their 30s. President Barack Obama appointed just nine judges younger than 40 during his two terms. A judge in his or her 30s can remain in place for as long as 60 years — there are multiple sitting judges in their 90s and one who is 102 — allowing the president who appointed them to leave a particularly long-lasting imprint on the courts. "President Trump selects highly-qualified and credentialed judicial nominees who have passed the White House's rigorous vetting process. Wherever there are judicial vacancies, President Trump will select highly qualified nominees with great respect for our Constitution and rule of law to be confirmed expeditiously," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. Trump's young nominees include Samuel Adkisson, an associate in the White House Counsel's Office who was 33 when Trump nominated him — making him one of the youngest people ever nominated to the federal bench. In his social media post announcing Adkisson's nomination, which is currently pending in the Senate, Trump praised his work on a case that resulted in the Supreme Court widening the president's power to control executive branch agencies. "Sam Adkisson is one of the brightest young conservative lawyers in the country and has been a standout member of the White House Counsel's Office. He will make an outstanding judge on the Eastern District of Tennessee," Bis said. Earlier this week, Adkisson's confirmation hearing was delayed after Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn declined to sign off on his nomination, using a procedural maneuver as one of his home-state senators. She hasn't explained why. "I think both parties, but especially Donald Trump in his second term, are placing a premium on youth because younger judges serve for longer and exert greater influence over important issues that come before the courts," said David Lat, a lawyer-turned-writer who publishes a Substack on legal affairs called Original Jurisdiction. John Michael Vazquez, who was the youngest district judge in New Jersey when he joined the bench in 2016 at 45 years old, said young judges can still have the experience they need to do the job well. "You can have somebody get out of law school at 25, and try a number of cases, appear in court regularly, and understand the dynamics of how a court works — those things that you can only gain through experience, you can't really gain through a textbook," said Vazquez, who is retired from the bench. "I do think that's critically important because it informs, ultimately, the most important aspect in my view of being a judge, which is your judgment." But some young jurists have acknowledged that their age has been held against them. Obama nominee Edmond E. Chang became the youngest serving federal judge in the country when he was confirmed in 2010. He said lawyers appearing before him would sometimes attempt "what I call Jedi mind tricks" to take advantage of his youth. "I do believe that the relative youth at the time did cause some lawyers to treat me differently than other judges; that they would try to navigate around decisions or rulings," Chang said in 2024. "They'll make an argument, deliver it with such confidence, hoping to – I thought – to kind of misdirect a new judge, and a youthful one at that, into their position when it was just – no, it was just wrong." Trump, though, went even younger. Kathryn Kimball Mizelle claimed the title of youngest federal judge in 2020, when Trump nominated her to a Florida court at age 33. During her confirmation process, the American Bar Association deemed her "not qualified, " largely due to what it described as her lack of experience. Asked about this during her confirmation hearing, Mizelle replied : "I can just point to my record, in-court litigation, and to the support that I have from over 200 attorneys that have submitted letters to this committee, explaining that they've worked with me, they've witnessed my abilities, my work product, my integrity, and they support my nomination." In 2018, Trump nominated Allison Jones Rushing, then 36, to the 4th Circuit Court of Appeals, making her the youngest circuit court judge confirmed in more than 15 years. At the time, her nomination spurred Orin Kerr, a professor at Stanford Law School, to question the wisdom of placing such a young person on the federal appellate bench. "Being a judicial-restraint-oriented type myself, I worry about judges getting rather intoxicated with the judicial power," Kerr wrote. "And I would guess that there is some correlation between the age a person became a judge and how tempted they are to drink enthusiastically from the tap of judicial power."
